questions.title: How does exponential gating enable revision of stored values in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces exponential activation functions for the input and forget gates in sLSTM (Eq. 3). I understand that this allows gates to take values larger than 1, but I am unclear on how exactly this solves the "inability to revise storage decisions" problem demonstrated with the Nearest Neighbor Search task. Could someone walk through a concrete example of how an exponential input gate can overwrite a previously stored value while still preserving gradient flow?

questions.title: What is the role of the normalizer state \(n_t\) in sLSTM and mLSTM?
questions.question_body: Both sLSTM (Eq. 3) and mLSTM (Eq. 7) maintain a normalizer state \(n_t\) that accumulates products of input gates and forget gates. The paper says it "sums up the product of the input gate times all future forget gates" and is used for scaling the hidden state. How is \(n_t\) computed in practice, why is it needed, and what would happen if we omitted this normalization step?

questions.title: How does the stabilizer state \(m_t\) prevent overflow in exponential gates?
questions.question_body: Equation 4 defines a stabilizer state \(m_t = \max(\log(f_t) + m_{t-1}, \log(i_t))\) and then rescales the gates to \(i'_t\) and \(f'_t\). I am confused about why this max operation works and how it guarantees that the exponentials stay within a numerically stable range. Is this equivalent to subtracting a running log‑max across time steps?

questions.title: Why does mLSTM use a matrix memory \(\mathbf{C}_t\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) instead of a vector?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that increasing the memory from a scalar to a matrix boosts storage capacity, especially for rare token prediction. Could someone explain intuitively how a covariance update \(\mathbf{C}_t = f_t \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + i_t \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top\) stores more information than a scalar cell, and how retrieval via \(\mathbf{C}_t \mathbf{q}_t\) works in practice?

questions.title: What does "memory mixing" mean for sLSTM, and how does it differ from hidden‑hidden connections in vanilla LSTM?
questions.question_body: Section 2.2 mentions that sLSTM can have multiple memory cells with recurrent matrices \(\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{z}}, \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{i}}, \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{f}}, \mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{o}}\) and that exponential gating changes their effect. How is this different from the standard hidden‑to‑gate connections in Eq. 2, and why does it enable new forms of state tracking?

questions.title: How are heads implemented in sLSTM and why are they not allowed to mix memories across heads?
questions.question_body: The paper states that sLSTM can have multiple heads with memory mixing within each head but not across heads, whereas for mLSTM heads are equivalent to multiple cells. What is the exact architecture of a head (e.g., separate gate parameters, separate normalizer?), and what is the motivation for prohibiting cross‑head mixing?

questions.title: Can you clarify the relationship between the covariance update rule and Fast Weight Programmers?
questions.question_body: In Section 2.3 it is mentioned that the matrix update \(\mathbf{C}_t = \mathbf{C}_{t-1} + \mathbf{v}_t \mathbf{k}_t^\top\) is equivalent to Fast Weight Programmers (FWP). How does the addition of decay/learning rates via forget and input gates map onto the classic FWP formulation? Are there any subtle differences in training dynamics?

questions.title: Why does mLSTM’s retrieval denominator use \(\max\{|\mathbf{n}_t^\top \mathbf{q}_t|, 1\}\)?
questions.question_body: The hidden state computation in Eq. 7 divides by the maximum of the absolute dot product between normalizer and query and 1. What is the intuition behind this clipping, and how sensitive is performance to the chosen threshold (default 1.0)?

questions.title: How does the pre‑up‑projection vs post‑up‑projection block affect sLSTM vs mLSTM performance?
questions.question_body: The authors use post up‑projection blocks for sLSTM and pre up‑projection blocks for mLSTM (Section 2.4). What exactly are these two designs, and why is one more suitable for scalar memory while the other benefits matrix memory?

questions.title: In the ablation study, how much does exponential gating contribute versus matrix memory?
questions.question_body: Table 2 (top) shows stepwise morphing from vanilla LSTM to xLSTM. However, I’m not sure whether the performance gain is mainly due to exponential gating, matrix memory, or their interaction. Could someone break down the individual contribution numbers or suggest an experiment to isolate each factor?

questions.title: What are the theoretical limitations of sLSTM’s non‑parallelizability?
questions.question_body: The paper notes that sLSTM cannot be parallelized because of memory mixing, yet they provide a fast CUDA kernel that is only twice slower than mLSTM. How does this kernel achieve parallelism across time steps (e.g., using scan operations), and what are the fundamental algorithmic barriers that prevent full parallelization?

questions.title: How does xLSTM compare to Retention or RWKV on formal language tasks requiring state tracking?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 shows xLSTM solving parity-like tasks while Transformers/SSMs fail. The caption mentions "state tracking" as a key advantage. Could someone elaborate on why exponential gating plus memory mixing gives xLSTM an edge over Retention or RWKV, which also have gating mechanisms?
